entries.title: Final rankings for the boys high school basketball Class of 2026
entries.summary: <p>When analyzing and evaluating the graduating senior class in Illinois, a narrative developed over the past couple of years: improvement.</p><p>The positive progress this group showed stood out as there were more Division I prospects — currently 24 and still counting — than originally anticipated.</p><p>At the top of the class, it can still be debated as to who the top prospect is in the state.</p><p>Here is the final look at the Class of 2026 in Illinois as they head off to join their respective college basketball programs this summer.</p><p><b>1. Jamison White, 6-8, East St. Louis</b></p><p>White made the most of his one year in Illinois, leading the Flyers to a 3A state title and to the top of the player rankings. He’s blessed with a strong, athletic frame while showcasing offensive tools, both in the post and facing the basket. Previously committed to Penn State, White will instead stay home and play at Saint Louis.</p><p><b>2. Lincoln Williams, 6-6, Kankakee</b></p><p>With size, length, athleticism and fluidity, Williams brings the physical attributes that stand out at the next level. Add in impressive production — the big wing averaged 24 points a game and became the Kays’ all-time leading scorer — and Williams is an enticing, high-upside prospect who remains uncommitted.</p><p><b>3. Mason Lockett, 6-5, Oswego East</b></p><p>Lockett is a potential jack-of-all-trades player with versatility at the next level. The DePaul recruit’s size on the perimeter and feel for the game is enough for him to continue ascending while his jumper gains dependability.</p><p><b>4. Marquis Clark, 6-1, Young</b></p><p>Following a November commitment to Tennessee, the tough, shifty Clark carried the Dolphins this season with huge numbers and monster games. The compact point guard will burst through an open seam in getting to the rim and has a lethal capacity for scoring the basketball.</p><p><b>5. Rashaun Porter, 6-7, DePaul Prep</b></p><p>The ultimate winner who checks off so many boxes when it comes to intangibles and impacting a game. An elite defender and tough rebounder, Porter was a huge recruiting win for Toledo.</p><p><b>6. Christopher Kirkpatrick, 6-3, New Trier</b></p><p>While an injury derailed his senior season, the Princeton recruit shined when healthy. Plays with an air of confidence. With step-back jumpers, solid footwork and smarts, he will hunt shots and is renowned for his comfort level in shooting the basketball from deep.</p><p><b>7. EJ Hazelett, 6-6, Kankakee</b></p><p>What you like about Hazelett are the ready-made skills as a scorer, combining both shooting range and physicality and touch around the basket. Headed to Indiana State.</p><p><b>8. Chris Bolte, 6-6, St. Ignatius</b></p><p>There is so much appeal when it comes to Bolte, who can play inside and out and impact the game in so many ways. The Yale recruit plays with all-out effort and a competitive spirit that can lift a team.</p><p><b>9. Rykan Woo, 5-11, DePaul Prep</b></p><p>The efficient scoring lead guard is still developing his point guard acumen, but he’s well schooled, intelligent and operates like he’s seen it all before. There is no doubting his ability to make a variety of shots — tough shots and in an efficient manner. Woo will play in the Ivy League at Brown.</p><p><b>10. Cooper Knowles, 6-9, West Hancock</b></p><p>Headed to Belmont, Knowles is a player who has always flown under the radar playing at a small school in the southwestern part of the state. Long, rangy, light on his feet and explosive off the floor, Knowles has a long way to go from a strength standpoint, but he’s just scratching the surface as a player.</p><p><b>11. Colin Stack, 7-1, Benet</b></p><p>While he may lack ideal post skills right now, Stack has soft finishing touch around the basket and face-up ability out to the three-point line. And when weight and strength are added, the potential is there to be a bonafide rim protector with his size and length. Stack has signed with North Dakota State.</p><p><b>12. Semaj Stampley, 6-1, Alton</b></p><p>A super offensive threat as a deadly shooter who connected on nearly 300 three-pointers in his career. Then he will surprise you with his more-than-you-think athleticism. South Dakota State landed a good one.</p><p><b>13. Jordan Williams, 6-5, Fremd</b></p><p>The Illinois State-bound Williams’ game is unassuming, but he’s a versatile wing who will stuff a stat sheet while providing high-level defense. Always engaged with an ideal demeanor and presence, Williams is all about doing what helps a team win.</p><p><b>14. Ben Okoro, 6-7, O’Fallon</b></p><p>The physical makeup is impressive. With his size and length as a run and jump athlete, Okoro’s ceiling is considerably high. While he needs to improve his perimeter shot, the Wisconsin-Milwaukee recruit uses his bounce off the floor and activity level to score at the rim and in transition.</p><p><b>15. Amir Danforth, 6-1, Rockford Auburn</b></p><p>What a career Danforth, who is headed to North Dakota State, put together. All he did was score 2,000-plus points and drain 300 three-pointers while emerging as one of the most lethal shooters in the state. He constantly puts pressure on opposing defenses with his quick release.<br></p>

entries.title: Obama Center releases grand opening weekend events schedule
entries.summary: <p>The Obama Presidential Center is preparing a big show for its grand opening next month.</p><p>The Center on Wednesday released its schedule of activities for its opening weekend on June 19-21. Many of the events are free, family-friendly and available to the public.</p><p>The activities in the 19-acre campus at 6001 S. Stony Island Ave. — ranging from live music, to dancing and face painting — may be the closest many people can get to being inside the Center's 225-foot museum tower for months to come. Tickets for opening weekend <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/06/obama-presidential-center-tickets-sales-demand-sold-out-june-july" target="_blank" >sold out in hours</a>, and reservations for Illinois Free Days (on Tuesdays) sold out past October.</p><p>Entertainment at the Center, under construction since 2021, will also feature "sports and play stations" at its Home Court athletic center. Expect to see mascots from the Chicago Bears, Blackhawks, Bulls, Cubs and White Sox, among others.</p><p>The museum debuts June 18 with an invitation-only grand opening ceremony, then opens to the public the next day — Juneteenth, on Friday, June 19. The public events will carry through that Sunday, which is Father's Day.</p><p>The idea behind the grand opening bash is to propel the center's mission to inspire and empower visitors.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/12/08/obama-presidential-center-home-court-building-opened-exclusive-look" target="_blank" >Obama Presidential Center’s first building is complete — Here’s an exclusive look</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/11/13/obama-presidential-center-jackson-park-delays-construction" target="_blank" >Obama Presidential Center takes shape after 10 years of delays and construction</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“These celebratory programs are only the beginning of the fun ways in which we will welcome visitors to campus. We will foster a spirit of civic engagement and joy," Valerie Jarrett, CEO of the Obama Foundation, said in a statement.</p><p>Other activities on opening weekend include:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-525996c0-59e2-11f1-b79b-81d176c0d80e"><li>Performances and programs featuring Obama Presidential Center commissioned artists;</li><li>Storytime and hands-on activities at the Center’s Chicago Public Library branch;</li><li>Double Dutch performances and hands-on crochet jump rope-making in Home Court;</li><li>Interactive experiences in the Fruit and Vegetable Garden centered on growing food and holistic well-being;</li><li>Talks in the Center’s auditorium;</li><li>Guided and self-guided audio tours of campus.</li></ul><p>The Center is planning for additional events after opening weekend, and throughout the summer:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-525996c1-59e2-11f1-b79b-81d176c0d80e"><li>In July and August, the Center will host a “You Are America” summer series of talks, films and community events for the nation's 250th anniversary. That series will kick off with a free Independence Day celebration called “The People’s Fourth,” featuring live music, self-guided tours and family-friendly activities.</li><li>Summer Garden Gatherings will be hosted in the Eleanor Roosevelt Fruit and Vegetable Garden every other week from July 12 to Sept. 20, in partnership with Urban Growers Collective.</li><li>On Aug. 4, an all-ages celebration of President Obama’s birthday will be held with a karaoke DJ set.</li><li>A 50-year-old-and-up walk-run club called At Your Pace will meet Thursday mornings from Aug. 6 to Oct. 8.</li></ul><p>Information about all Obama Presidential Center programming will be available on the Foundation’s website and event calendar and will be updated as programs are added. Check it out at <a class="Link" href="https://obama.org/" target="_blank" >Obama.org</a>.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally stabbed in Greater Grand Crossing over Memorial Day weekend
entries.summary: <p>Detectives are investigating the fatal stabbing of a 47-year-old man Monday morning in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood. </p><p>His death occurred during the <a class="Link" href="2 dead, 38 wounded in Memorial Day weekend shootings in Chicago" target="_blank" >long Memorial Day holiday weekend,</a> in which 38 people were wounded in shootings and two people died after being shot, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/man-charged-in-death-of-2-year-old-boy-who-fatally-shot-himself-in-pullman" target="_blank" >including a toddler.</a></p><p>The still-unidentified 47-year-old man was attacked and found unresponsive inside an apartment in the 400 block of East 73rd Street, police said. </p><p>The man, who was pronounced dead on the scene, died of multiple sharp force injuries and his death was ruled a homicide, according to a Tuesday autopsy performed by the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Cubs analyst Jim Deshaies on the 'W' he had to have (take that, Nolan Ryan) 40 years ago this week
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> TV analyst Jim Deshaies took a few minutes Tuesday to scroll through Baseball Reference’s “Today in Baseball History” page, something he’d done many times before. Mining for a nugget that might fit into that night’s broadcast is never a bad idea, especially when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" target="_blank" >the team is bordering on unwatchable</a>.</p><p>He saw the name of Ty Cobb, who recorded his 1,000th extra-base hit on March 26, 1925, against the White Sox. And the name of Josh Gibson, who on that same date in 1946 homered for the Homestead Grays at Yankee Stadium. And that of Hank Aaron, who in 1969 swatted his 500th double to go with his 519 homers at the time.</p><p>Great stuff. What’s better than nerding out about baseball?</p><p>The 65-year-old southpaw scrolled on, and there it was:“1986 — Houston Astros pitcher Jim Deshaies records his first major league win.”</p><p>How about that?</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" >Cubs’ skid reaches 10 as Pirates score early and often</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/24/cubs-astros-wrigley-field-chicago-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga-pete-crow-armstrong" target="_blank" >Cubs can’t stop losing — but other than that, everything’s fine</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It was 40 years to the day since Deshaies toed the rubber in St. Louis, struck out 10 Cardinals hitters — slugger Jack Clark three times — and got himself off the schneid in his fifth start of the season and the seventh of his career.</p><p>It’s safe to say the details of that game aren’t burned into Deshaies’ brain.</p><p>“Had I not seen it today and if someone would’ve asked me who my first win came against, I don’t think I would have known,” he said.</p><p>What he does remember, though, is the feeling he had early on as a rookie that his leash was short. He’d won a three-man battle for the Astros’ final rotation spot that had lasted all of spring training, and it was a team and a veteran rotation — with Nolan Ryan going strong at 39, and eventual 1986 Cy Young winner Mike Scott and Bob Knepper also in their 30s — built to win now.</p><p>“Nobody had said anything to me, but I felt pressure,” Deshaies said. “I hadn’t had a win yet, and it was Memorial Day. I didn’t know if I might get shipped out.”</p><p>In the last days of spring training in Kissimmee, Florida, Deshaies had braced for news — good or bad — from manager Hal Lanier. Instead, Lanier never got around to telling him he’d made the team. As Deshaies’ wife, Lori, prepared to hit the road from Kissimmee a day or two ahead of the team for wherever they’d be living, Deshaies told her, “Just head toward Houston.” If it was going to be the Triple-A Tucson (Arizona) Toros, she could simply keep barreling west on Interstate 10.</p><p>It turned out nicely that year for Deshaies, who won 12 games — at the time, the Astros’ rookie record — on a 96-win team that ran away with the National League West by 10 games only to be felled by the glory-bound Mets in the NLCS.</p><p>Deshaies was even more effective for the Astros in 1988 and especially in 1989, when he posted career bests in wins (15), ERA (2.91), innings (225⅔) and strikeouts (153). He later pitched for the Padres, Giants, Twins and Phillies and retired in 1995 with 84 wins in 257 appearances, 253 of them starts.</p><p>But his favorite start? That came in his rookie season, and it wasn’t his maiden “W” in St. Louis. It was in late September in Houston against the Dodgers, whom Deshaies mowed through in a two-hit shutout, striking out the first eight hitters he faced — at the time, a major league record — and 10 in all. It put him in double digits in wins and gave him a sense that maybe, just maybe, he was where he belonged even if he wasn’t as dominant as Scott or as awe-inspiring as the godlike Ryan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/CBhHfwN9d0M?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Deshaies' eighth K in a row to start game"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“I was intimidated by Nolan, star-struck by Nolan,” Deshaies said. “He’d walk through the clubhouse and you’d just kind of watch him. It was an out-of-body, surreal-type experience.”</p><p>Exactly one night after Deshaies’ finest outing, Ryan started against the Giants and allowed one hit and no runs, blowing away 12 batters.</p><p>“After that one, I joked to Alan Ashby, our catcher, ‘You’d think he’d let me have the spotlight for once,’ ” Deshaies said. “But ‘Ash’ said, ‘You watch, Scott’s going to be even better tomorrow.’ ”</p><p>Anyone want to guess what Scott pulled off the next day?</p><p>Hint: It rhymes with “no quitter.”</p><p>And not only that, but Scott’s 13-strikeout no-no clinched the division title.</p><p>Jim De-who?</p><p>“Those guys were great,” Deshaies said.</p><p>Heck of a thing to be a part of for a 25-year-old just starting to find his way.</p><p>It all goes back to that first “W.” Deshaies is pretty sure he possesses a baseball from that game, though where it might be is another matter. He’s certain there was no beer shower in the clubhouse to celebrate his win, or anything else along the lines of what players do now. Lori was in Houston watching the game on TV. Deshaies is just about certain his older brother, Mike, wasn’t in the stands in St. Louis, because Mike went to a lot of his games and little bro always seemed to lose them.</p><p>Ah, well. So it wasn’t the biggest night of Deshaies’ life.</p><p>Forty years later, though, how nice to be able to look back on it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-h/" target="_blank" >Mariah Woelfel</a></h5><p><b>Mayor in Rome</b>: Mayor Brandon Johnson has a meeting Thursday with the world's most famous Chicagoan: Pope Leo XIV. He will be the latest Illinoisan to meet the pope, who has given locals from his hometown, including Gov. JB Pritzker, private audiences since starting his papal ministry a year ago.</p><p><b>Papal plan</b>: Johnson plans to thank Pope Leo for his advocacy, which includes pushing back against the U.S. war in Iran, calling for peace in Gaza and criticizing President Donald Trump’s immigration policies. The meeting comes as Johnson attempts to shore up his political base before what's sure to be a tough reelection battle, though the mayor hasn't announced a bid yet.</p><p><b>The itinerary</b>: On Wednesday, a 50-member delegation will tour the town with members of Rome's City Council. Johnson is set to arrive Thursday and meet the pope at 3:30 p.m., when he plans to <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-k/" target="_blank" >present the pontiff with a jar of giardiniera</a>. Then Johnson will hold press conference at American University, and later has scheduled a fireside chat and dinner. On Friday, Johnson plans to tour a new Metro station and an affordable housing project with Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri.</p><p><a class="Link" >Here are the candidates for Chicago’s first-ever elected school board president</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yd/" target="_blank" >Sarah Karp</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yh/" target="_blank" >Emmanuel Camarillo</a></h5><p><b>In the running</b>: Tuesday was the petition filing deadline to enter the race for a seat on Chicago’s first fully elected school board. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yk/" target="_blank" >Fifty-one candidates are officially in the running</a>. All 20 district seats and the citywide president position will be up for grabs in the Nov. 3 election. Voters will get to cast a ballot for a school board member in their community and for the president.</p><p><b>Race for prez</b>: Five people are running for board president, a powerful position that holds sway over what the board debates and votes on. Four of them — Jessica Biggs, Jennifer Custer, former board member Sendhil Revuluri and attorney Victor Henderson — submitted petitions the first day and will face off in a lottery to get the top spot on the ballot. Hilario Dominguez, deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union and the CTU's preferred candidate, submitted his petition Tuesday.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: November’s election and the transition from a partially elected, partially appointed board marks the culmination of years of work by advocates. target="_blank" >Inside the making of a Second City show</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tr/" target="_blank" >Mike Davis</a></h5><p>It’s a typical afternoon in April. Onstage at Second City, just after lunchtime, six actors are rehearsing a sketch for its newest show, "Pandemonium, Please Hold."</p><p>Being in the room for a Second City rehearsal is a stark contrast to traditional theater, whose rehearsals include a lot of dead air with actors standing around doing nothing as crew members problem-solve lighting, sound and technical issues.</p><p>But here, rehearsal is exciting. When director Carisa Barreca pauses a scene to give notes, the performers immediately start riffing. Ideas and jokes are flying in every direction. At one point, cast member Zoe McKee breaks out into song. It’s beautiful, but Barreca eventually reigns them in.</p><p>How do you problem-solve funny? How does Second City, a company known for being the training ground for sketch comedy legends, create skits that work? It all starts in the rehearsal room.</p><p>WBEZ got a behind-the-scenes look at the making of the now open show. You can <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-ty/" target="_blank" >read about it here</a>, or <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tj/" target="_blank" >listen to the audio story here</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tt/" target="_blank" ><b>MORE HERE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>WBEZ reporter Mariah Woelfel and Sun-Times photojournalist Zubaer Khan are in Rome to cover Mayor Johnson's meeting with Pope Leo XIV. We're looking for your Rome recommendations to send them for their off-hours. Where should they go? What should they eat?</p><p>We want to know: What would you do in Rome? Tell us why.</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email your answer here</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story. Tell us your name and neighborhood so we can shout you out.</i></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE CHICAGO 📸</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b20000" name="image-b20000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c506714/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bbc6b26/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/62bad30/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A haze hangs over Chicago’s downtown area seen from the air near the 8700 block of South Jeffery Blvd, Tuesday, May 26, 2026. entries.title: Metra adding trains to Rock Island, Electric lines as part of new transit law requirement
entries.summary: <p>Metra is adding several daily train runs to its Rock Island District line starting June 1, the first step in schedule adjustments required by the Northern Illinois Transit Authority law that goes into effect the same day.</p><p>The commuter rail agency is adding four late-day daily train trips on weekdays and 18 more weekend train trips. The Rock Island line is also phasing out "flag stops," which require a customer to wave down a train for it to stop at a station, in favor of standard stops. Some stops have been dropped from the schedule due to low ridership.</p><p>The idea, Metra CEO Jim Derwinski said in a board meeting last week, is to move toward "regional rail service." Regional rail service means more frequent all-day trains, a shift away from the agency's 9-to-5 commuter schedule. The NITA law requires that Metra implement regional rail service pilots on the Rock Island and Metra Electric lines.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Under fire over tainted ‘Broadview 6’ case, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor outlines ‘sweeping’ reforms
entries.summary: <p>Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros announced<b> </b>“sweeping internal reforms”<b> </b>Wednesday<b> </b>to his office’s grand jury practices, in the wake of the “Broadview Six” scandal that has shaken the city’s federal courthouse.</p><p>Boutros also announced that he and the Justice Department had taken “swift action related to internal personnel matters,” though he didn’t share additional details. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >The “Broadview Six” case fell apart</a>, days before trial, after a judge discovered improprieties during grand jury proceedings. The alleged misconduct came to light only after a lengthy push by defense attorneys to get the judge to review unredacted transcripts of what occurred.</p><p>The allegations included a prosecutor improperly putting her personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges, a prosecutor having substantive contact with grand jurors outside the grand jury room, and a prosecutor excusing grand jurors who disagreed with the case.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/05/26/broadview-six-andrew-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago" >Grand jurors in tainted ‘Broadview 6' case had contact with Chicago’s top federal prosecutor, defense says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros’ office said in a press release Wednesday that the new process “will be more transparent, effective, and impactful while greatly reducing the likelihood of mistakes and errors.”<b> </b>It also said “many”<b> </b>of the reforms “are being implemented for the first time anywhere in the country.”</p><p>Still, the most specific reform identified by Boutros was “extensive, deep-dive training from national experts outside the office.” </p><p>That’s perhaps because of the secrecy that traditionally surrounds the grand jury process.</p><p>“These remediations should also be deeply curative and put to rest once and for all the divergent practices that have existed across the office for decades, including from one assistant U.S. attorney to another as well as from one generation to the next,” Boutros said. “That’s because these are clear, bright line rules that everyone must abide by, which should streamline and simplify the decision-making and disclosure process, as opposed to bedevil it.”</p><p>Boutros also acknowledged that, as part of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/22/broadview-six-federal-prosecutors-misconduct-tainted-cases-reviewed" target="_blank" >previously announced review</a> prompted by the “Broadview Six” case, defense attorneys in cases that might have been similarly tainted will receive transcripts — or “minutes” — from grand jury proceedings.</p><p>Charged in the “Broadview Six” case were former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, former Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician Joselyn Walsh and onetime Abughazaleh campaign worker Andre Martin.</p><p>They were accused of joining a larger crowd that surrounded an immigration agent’s vehicle last September. The crowd pushed, scratched<b> </b>and<b> </b>otherwise damaged the agent’s SUV. Of that crowd, federal prosecutors charged only six people, all largely involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >selective prosecution</a> and freedom of expression.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >Charges were dropped</a> against Sharp and Walsh in March. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >The remaining case was dismissed</a> last week after it was reduced to a misdemeanor matter.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" >‘Broadview Six’ charges dropped as Chicago’s top federal prosecutor admits case was tainted by misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Questions have since emerged about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/26/broadview-six-loretto-hosptial-ice-sheri-mecklenburg-andrew-boutros" target="_blank" >a separate prosecution</a>, involving former Loretto Hospital Chief Financial Officer Anosh<b> </b>Ahmed. Defense attorneys for a co-defendant of Ahmed’s are seeking permanent dismissal of the charges against their client, though no such motion has yet to be filed on behalf of Ahmed.</p><p>The former lead prosecutor in the "Broadview Six" case, Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg, also formerly handled the case against Ahmed. She left earlier this year to serve as counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee, though she's since been terminated from that role. Also involved in the "Broadview Six" prosecution were assistant U.S. attorneys William<b> </b>Hogan, Matthew<b> </b>Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez.</p><p>After the revelations in the "Broadview Six" case went public, Boutros sent an internal email to his office calling the three remaining prosecutors "courageous"<b> </b>for fighting "long and hard for a case they inherited when a colleague departed the office."</p>

entries.title: Family devastated after Tilden High honor roll student fatally shot while walking to school
entries.summary: <p>When Asucena Velazquez hugged her 17-year-old son before he left for school Tuesday morning, she never imagined he wouldn’t return home.</p><p>Pedro Ramirez was on his way from their Back of the Yards home to class at Tilden High School when he was fatally shot in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/17-year-old-boy-killed-2-critically-wounded-in-back-of-the-yards-shooting" target="_blank" >5000 block of South Throop Street</a>.</p><p>“It never crossed my mind that my boy would get hurt going to school,” Velazquez told the Sun-Times. “They robbed my son of his future,” Velazquez said.</p><p>Around 7:40 a.m. a stolen black Jeep Cherokee with four masked assailants inside stopped behind a southbound red minivan near 51st Street, according to a police report. At least two of them got out of the Jeep brandishing a "long gun," and "fired dozens of rifle rounds" in the minivan's direction.</p><p>The two men who were inside the red minivan, 55 and 61, were shot but were able to drive away and call 911 for help — but the two-sport Tilden athlete and honor roll student collapsed. </p><p>"During the barrage of gunfire, the victim, who was walking westbound on the south side of 51st Street was inadvertently struck one time in the right side," the report said. He was pronounced dead at 8:20 a.m. at Comer Children's Hospital. </p><p>Both men were take to Stroger Hospital. The 55-year-old man has since been released, while the 65-year-old is still hospitalized in stable condition.</p><p>A 911 caller who witnessed the attack gave police a description of the Jeep. Officers then chase it and took one of the four occupants of the Jeep into custody near 44th Street and Wolcott Avenue. The other three assailants got away on foot, according to the report. One pistol and one rifle were found in the Jeep. </p><p>Velazquez said she was at home when she got a call from the hospital that Pedro had been hurt in a shooting. When she arrived she said doctors told her Pedro died from his injuries.</p><p>Pedro’s death has left their family devastated, Velazquez said.</p><p>“He was a good boy,” said Velazquez. “He was respectful and caring. He didn’t mess with anyone.”</p><p>Velazquez said she wants justice for her son and hopes police will find those responsible.</p><p>A person of interest has been taken into custody, police said, but no charges had been filed as of Wednesday morning.</p><p>Pedro, who was born in Mexico and moved to the U.S. at 5 years old, was a junior at Tilden, where he played on both the soccer and volleyball teams.</p><p>His mother said he had dreams of going to college and studying engineering.</p><p>In the hours after his death, Velazquez said she’s received an overwhelming amount of support from Pedro’s friends and the community.</p><p>She said her son’s friends have stopped by and offered their condolences.</p><p>“His friends are destroyed,” Velazquez said. “I always knew he had a lot of friends, but I didn’t realize how much they loved him. But they’ve shown me that my son was an excellent friend and classmate. He was in the wrong place at the wrong time.'' </p><p>A GoFundMe to help Pedro’s family with funeral expenses can be found <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/apoyo-para-la-familia-de-pedrito?attribution_id=sl:a1a4eb96-1fef-4342-9cb1-5493dac673ca&lang=en_US&ts=1779838447&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp17_ta-amp20_t1&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=copy_link" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p>

entries.title: Estudiante de CPS regresa junto a su madre en Chicago tras ser liberado de detención migratoria
entries.summary: <p>Un estudiante de último año de la secundaria Mather, detenido por agentes federales junto a su madre en marzo, regresa a casa en Chicago.</p><p>Ricardo Navarrete, de 18 años, compareció en una audiencia de fianza ante la corte de inmigración el martes por la mañana y fue liberado de la custodia federal, según Kelli Fennell, abogada de la familia.</p><p>“Estamos felices de que esté de camino a casa para reunirse con su familia”, dijo Fennell en un comunicado enviado por correo electrónico.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los agentes de inmigración detuvieron a Ricardo y a su madre durante una comparecencia rutinaria en la corte por su caso de asilo en marzo. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/20/juez-ordena-la-liberacion-de-una-mama-de-cps-detenida-por-ice-su-hijo-adolescente-sigue-detenido" target="_blank" >La semana pasada, Liliana Navarrete fue una de las 18 personas liberadas</a> mediante una moción de hábeas corpus presentada ante un juez federal en Kentucky.</p><p>La lucha por su caso de inmigración continuará en las cortes de Chicago, han dicho sus abogados.</p><p>Ricardo y Liliana tenían una solicitud de asilo activa cuando fueron detenidos, y ninguno de los dos tiene antecedentes criminales, según los abogados de la familia. Madre e hijo llegaron a Chicago en 2022 como solicitantes de asilo provenientes de Colombia.</p><p>Su liberación marca una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >victoria para los amigos, familiares y otros que realizaron</a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >manifestaciones</a> y hablaron con varios medios de comunicación, esperando que la atención ayudara a traer de regreso a la madre y al hijo a Chicago.</p><p>Ricardo se perdió el baile de graduación de Mather la semana pasada, pero hay una posibilidad de que pueda regresar a tiempo para caminar sobre el escenario en su ceremonia de graduación el jueves.</p><p>El destacado jugador de fútbol se había comprometido a jugar para el prestigioso Truman College después de graduarse, pero esos planes han estado en el aire desde que él y su madre fueron detenidos.</p><p>Ricardo había descrito las difíciles condiciones en las instalaciones de detención a amigos y familiares, incluyendo haber sido mantenido en cuartos estrechos con docenas de hombres, haber pasado tiempo en confinamiento solitario y haber dormido en el suelo sin cobija.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: A petting zoo, helicopter and wrestling match: Chicago Park District hosts first disabilities celebration
entries.summary: <p>While jumping in an Iron Man-themed bouncy house, high school students waved hello to a Chicago Police Department pilot flying a helicopter low above the first-ever Chicago Park District celebration of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.</p><p>The group from Percy Julian High School gathered alongside nearly 4,000 other people with cognitive disabilities at Maggie Daley Park and Butler Field to enjoy a petting zoo, a wrestling match, mini-golf and other activities Wednesday.</p><p>Emily Elzen, a Chicago Public Schools speech pathologist and supervisor for the far south side high schoolers, said the pilot’s wave and flashing lights from the helicopter were highlights for her students.</p><p>“You see the smiles that you’ve never seen before, and it makes you feel so good and realize that everybody deserves to be happy,” Elzen said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel </div><p>Special Children's Charities Executive Director Amy Taylor said the organization wanted to create a space where people with many different disabilities could partake in the fun.</p><p>“Traditionally, some of these events would be more athletics focused, and now we’ve opened this up,” Taylor said. “The biggest piece is just joy when walking through the parks seeing how excited and happy everyone is.”</p><p>Participants enjoyed arts and crafts, played BINGO, blew bubbles, posed in a photo booth and could take part in physical activities like rock climbing, adaptive bike riding and dancing.</p><p>“We just wanted to throw a big party for these guys at the end of the year to celebrate all their successes and celebrate, you know, all the hard work that they put in,” Park District Administrator Eileen Guinane said.</p><p>Guinane and Taylor both said they hope the celebration becomes an annual event.</p><p>With music blaring and bubbles still floating, students waved goodbye to CPD horses at around 1 p.m. before loading onto about 180 buses.</p><p>"We will be here again and again and again if we can," supervisor Elzen said. </p>

entries.title: Sen. Durbin delivers farewell address at state Capitol, warns legislators about threats to election integrity
entries.summary: <p>From legislation that banned smoking on domestic flights, to his continued push for Dreamers to live in the U.S. legally, retiring U.S Sen. Dick Durbin recalled the highlights of his 44 years of public service on Wednesday while also issuing a dire warning about this fall's midterm elections. </p><p>"Today we meet five months before a national election. Debates in Congress and contests in our courts indicate this next election may be challenged in ways we have never seen before in our history," Durbin said before the Illinois General Assembly in Springfield. "Abraham Lincoln, in the House Divided speech that he gave here in Springfield, gave a grim warning that the divisions in America over the issue of slavery could destroy our nation. Similar divisions today. The challenge we face in the days ahead could be just as serious. I hope that those of us blessed to live in this land of Lincoln will remember his warnings in 1858 and his counsel to those who lead this nation in our time."</p><p>Durbin, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/senator-dick-durbin-reelection" >announced last year </a>that he would step down after five terms in the U.S. Senate and seven terms in the U.S. House, also spoke about the void he'll feel come January. </p><p>"I think about what I'm going to miss the most about retirement is the fact that at least during this period of time as senator, I've had a chance to help so many people," Durbin said in a farewell address at the Illinois State Capitol. "I don't know that I will ever find anything that has such a dramatic impact on individuals and their opportunities and rights."</p><p>The Springfield native, 81, came to the Capitol for a rare joint session for legislators to salute his years of public service. Durbin was first lauded by legislators, including elected officials who once interned or worked for him, like State Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, and State Sen. Mike Simmons, D-Chicago. Gov. JB Pritzker also joined legislators on the House floor. Although members of the far right Illinois Freedom Caucus opted to skip the address, Durbin received a standing ovation from both parties after his 23-minute speech.</p><p>Durbin, who has introduced the Dream Act during every Congress since 2001, said he's still pushing for a legal path to citizenship for people who were brought to the U.S. as children. He last introduced the legislation in 2025 with co-sponsor U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska.</p><p>"I hope that you'll join me in that commitment. It was a bipartisan measure, and it should be a bipartisan measure," Durbin said. "These DACA people are serving America in so many ways, as teachers and doctors and nurses and policemen and members of our military, you name it. They're doing all those jobs. They just want a chance to be part of America, and it's not too much to ask."</p><p>Durbin also recalled his push to ban smoking on domestic flights, including being told by then-House Majority Whip Rep. Thomas Foley, D-Wash. in 1983 to "lay off of tobacco" to appease Southern Democrats. Durbin said his father died at age 53 of lung cancer after smoking two packs a day, and he vowed to never pick up the habit. His battle with big tobacco came to a head while sitting on a crowded flight from Phoenix to Chicago —  in a middle seat "between two chain smoking sumo wrestlers."</p><p>That led to legislation that Durbin sponsored in 1998 — initially banning smoking on domestic flights that were two hours or less. By 1990, it was expanded to nearly all domestic flights.</p><p>The senator also joked about "one of the most interesting" issues he's had to face: "to stop one damn fish from getting in Lake Michigan," he said of trying to keep Asian carp form reaching the Great Lakes. </p><p>"I can't tell you how many millions of dollars we've spent for poison, for electroshock, for disco bubble machines," Durbin said. "We've tried everything, and we've done it, but there's a major project that's still pending."</p><p>Buckner told the Sun-Times the senator deserves the same laurels reserved for Illinois political giants like former President Barack Obama and U.S. Sen. Paul Simon: "Durbin's name is in that group." </p><p>Now serving in the role of Speaker Pro Tempore, Buckner accidentally landed at Durbin’s office after receiving multiple job rejections out of college. He said seeing the senator be recognized by both chambers was a “full-circle” moment.</p><p>“I had nowhere to go and Dick Durbin gave me a call,” Buckner said. “He remembered me from when I interned with him and he brought me on. It really changed the trajectory of my life, so I’m forever in his debt.”</p><p><i>Tina Sfondeles reported from Chicago; Matt Trunfio reported from Springfield</i></p>

entries.title: Relax, the Cubs will be fine. After all, why wouldn't they be?
entries.summary: <p>Everybody calm down.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>, despite looking worse than a last-place 16-inch team at Oz Park during this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" target="_blank" >2-14 free-fall heading into Wednesday night’s game in Pittsburgh</a>, are going to be fine.</p><p>How can you not believe it if president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer, on whose watch the Cubs have won one playoff series and zero division titles since 2020, says it’s so?</p><p>“Everyone in there knows we’re going to play better,” Hoyer told reporters at PNC Park before the Cubs recommenced getting their brains beaten in, “but it’s just a matter of when and how that’s going to shake out.”</p><p>For one thing, you just know the Cubs are going to get back to playing their signature brand of stellar defense. Well, they probably will. A lot of it depends on whether or not center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, their most ballyhooed slinger of leather, stops insisting on inserting “Fool’s” before “Gold Glove.”</p><p>What’s eating Pete these days, anyway? Do the Cubs need to hire a personal care assistant (PCA) to keep an eye on him? Judging by his antics and errors in the outfield lately, he’s not exactly at the top of his mental game. The wheels are still turning, as the expression goes, but the hamster died.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" >Cubs’ skid reaches 10 as Pirates score early and often</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/24/cubs-astros-wrigley-field-chicago-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga-pete-crow-armstrong" target="_blank" >Cubs can’t stop losing — but other than that, everything’s fine</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ah, well, at least you know the Cubs’ pitching will only improve, and soon, in all likelihood in a big way. Maybe? Edward Cabrera should be back soon, although, come to think of it, he averaged three earned runs allowed in about five innings pitched in his last eight starts before a blister sidetracked him, and that really isn’t anything special. Matthew Boyd and his 6.00 ERA — surely misleading — shouldn’t be far behind Cabrera. Remember Justin Steele? If and when he comes back, one can only assume he’ll be as good as new if not better than ever. Right?</p><p>Of course Shota Imanaga will simply flip a switch and stop leaving meatballs in the zone. Of course veteran reliever Phil Maton will have a eureka moment and rediscover the art of — what’s it called again? — pitching. Of course Hoyer will make all the right moves to bolster the rotation and ’pen as needed, because when has he ever not come through before? (Did we already mention the playoff series win?)</p><p>As far as hitting, which has been the weakness of weaknesses for the Cubs since their 8-0 start to the month of May, let’s address it with a question: Are you familiar with the term “back of the baseball card”?</p><p>What it implies, essentially, is that the proven track records of the veterans in the Cubs’ lineup — particularly the ones making huge chunks of a $250 payroll — should allow worried fans to relax because, really, these season statistics practically write themselves.</p><p>No one should doubt the coming onslaught from the bat of $35 million-a-year third baseman Alex Bregman, for example. Yes, he so far is driving the ball with the authority of your Aunt Dotty, but just look at the back of the man’s card! In fact, one of us is doing it right now and seeing — hang on, really? — one All-Star appearance for Bregman and nothing higher than 19th in MVP voting since 2019. Again, really?</p><p>But there’s no reason shortstop Dansby Swanson, in year four of his $177 deal, won’t get hotter than Georgia asphalt with the stick just because he has a lower batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage, not to mention a higher strikeout rate, as a Cub than he had as a Brave.</p><p>And then there’s left fielder Ian Happ, the longest-tenured Cub, who came into Wednesday a mere 10 hits shy of 1,000 for his career, suggesting he has an excellent chance to reach the milestone by September. Happ did have an RBI double Tuesday in a 12-1 loss — the team’s 10th in a row — but then got gunned out at third on a highly questionable tag-up. In fairness to him, the whole thing had to be a bit confusing given how rarely he’d been on base with a hit lately.</p><p>The point being, again — everybody calm down.</p><p>OK, fine, so the Cubs have gone from first place to last place so fast, it’s almost like they’re the Pirates. Or the Cardinals. Or the Reds. Anyone else, really, aside from the Brewers.</p><p>But how afraid is anyone supposed to be of these first-place Brewers, anyway? What, just because they’ve made the National League Central their bully’s playground, smacking around the Cubs and all others with wanton abandon for most of this decade — most notably since Pat Murphy took over as manager — are we really expected to sit here and believe it might go down like that again in 2026?</p><p>Oh, please.</p><p>The highest-paid skipper in the game, meanwhile — the Cubs’ Craig Counsell, the pride of the Hoyer regime — just might be struggling a tiny bit himself. Counsell has gone from, roughly, “We’ll be fine” to, “It’s time to turn it up a notch” to, “For the love of God, will someone, anyone, grab a bat and at least appear to have a vague clue as to its general purpose?”</p><p>But fear not, because if anyone can save the day, it’s the guy with a .538 winning percentage as Cubs skipper, which is even better than the .531 he had in Milwaukee, where he led the Brewers to the postseason five times without getting to a World Series.</p><p>So, everybody just take a few deep breaths.</p><p>After all, what could go wrong?</p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: Mayor Johnson still opposed to stricter curfew and parent responsibility laws after holiday weekend mayhem
entries.summary: <p>Despite a Memorial Day weekend marred by teen takeovers turned violent, Mayor Brandon Johnson said Wednesday that stricter curfew and parental responsibility laws are not the answer to the perennial problem plaguing Chicago.</p><p>Johnson said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/cpd-officers-hurt-near-west-side-gathering" >15 arrests</a> were made early Sunday after a car veered into five Chicago police officers and injured them as they tried to disperse an unruly crowd of youths gathered on the Near West Side. But those arrests, he added, did not prevent an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/25/large-crowd-causes-lake-shore-drive-closure-at-57th-street" >even bigger crowd </a>from overtaking the 57th Street Beach in Hyde Park and spilling onto Lake Shore Drive on Memorial Day.</p><p>That tells the mayor throwing the book at young people and their parents is not the answer to the problem of unruly gatherings summoned by social media.</p><p>“I’ve said multiple times that they should be held accountable and that happened. What I also said was, if you look at other cities where they’ve had more aggressive responses to it, has it stopped it from happening? The answer is no,“ the mayor said. </p><p>“That’s why you can’t have just a one-sided, imbalanced approach. … If we believe that incarceration is the best way to keep people safe, America would be the safest place on the planet. We have more people locked up in America than anywhere in the planet and we are, by far not the safest place on the globe.”</p><p>Johnson said the “safest cities in America have one thing in common: They invest in people.” To underscore the point, he put up a chart that showed showed dramatic declines in shootings and homicides in neighborhoods where the city hired the greatest number of young people. </p><p>“We hold people accountable. But if we give them opportunity, we can create safer communities,” the mayor said. “My investments drive violence down… If it works, let’s do more of that."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a00000" name="image-a00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f3d2036/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6290611/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8037434/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mayor Brandon Johnson answers questions from the press during press conference at City Hall in the Loop, Wednesday, May 27, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8037434/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ea78913/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8037434/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1e%2Fdf%2Fa9323e784d08bbc997769f879350%2Fmayortakeovers-260528-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson answers questions at a City Hall press conference Wednesday, where he stressed that stricter curfew and parental responsibility laws are not the answer to teen takeovers. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Hyde Park Ald. Desmon Yancy (5th) said the Memorial Day gathering that swarmed Hyde Park in his ward was the “third event in less than a month," adding that police confiscated knives, guns, bear sprays and tasers. </p><p>“With that sort of weaponry, it’s clear that this is not about having a good time,” Yancy said. “While many of the young people who are participating in these mass gatherings are not the ones who are creating mayhem and mischief, there are those that are specifically there for that.”</p><p>Yancy said frustrated constituents and the police officers who serve them want more tools from the City Council to curb teen takeovers. </p><p>“We have a pretty wide net for kids with pretty big holes in it," he said. “I’m not usually a fan of punitive measures, but I don’t know that we have any other things at our disposal now."</p><p>Public Safety Committee Chair Brian Hopkins (2nd) said there is increasing support for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/21/brian-hopkins-curfew-ordinance-new-revision-mayor-brandon-johnson-teen-takeovers" >revised curfew ordinance,</a> additional parental responsibility measures, and for an attempt to hold social media companies accountable.</p><p>"The mayor needs to understand that the city is losing patience with our inability to prevent these teen takeovers from happening," Hopkins said. "For him to rule out effective tools when we need them is shortsighted and counter-productive."</p><p>Fraternal Order of Police President John Catanzara argued that Johnson’s “permissive” message is inviting more unruly groups of teenagers to “infringe on the rights” of law-abiding Chicagoans.</p><p>“If 15 arrests didn’t solve it the first time, then the next time, you arrest 30. And the next time, you arrest 60. Mob action is mob action,” Catanzara said.</p><p> "Kids just don’t seem to give a damn," Catanzara added. "It’s all about just taking over whatever spot they want, doing their little stupid TikTok to get more likes to be sensational and stupid and to hell with the rest of society. The only way it’s going to stop is if you start locking them all up and making their parents come and pick them up on the other side of the damned city.”</p><p>Former Chicago Police Superintendent Garry McCarthy's hard-nosed approach to unruly groups of young people largely succeeded in controlling the flash mobs that plagued Michigan Avenue during then Mayor Rahm Emanuel's tenure.</p><p>“I didn’t have a mayor like Brandon Johnson who made excuses,” McCarthy said.</p><p>“Let’s stop calling them teen takeovers. That is sending the wrong message. That sounds cute. These are mob actions. … There needs to be some sort of accountability for, not just the kids, but the parents and elected officials. Permissiveness is not working. It’s never worked. All it does is cause bad behavior.”</p>

entries.title: Stars' Mallory Swanson returns to USWNT
entries.summary: <p>Triple Espresso is back.</p><p>The trio of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Sophia Wilson, nicknamed Triple Espresso at the 2024 Olympics, were named on Tuesday to the U.S. training camp roster for a pair of June matches against the Brazilian national team in Brazil. The three have not played together since the gold-medal match at the Paris Games.</p><p>Swanson was included on the U.S. roster for the first time since October 2024. She recently returned to her club team, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/stars" >Stars</a>, after taking time off for the birth of her daughter in November.</p><p>The 28-year-old Swanson has 38 goals in 103 appearances with the national team and scored the lone goal in the 1-0 victory over Brazil for the gold medal in Paris.</p><p>Wilson had returned to the national team in April after taking maternity leave last year for the birth of her daughter. She has 24 goals in 61 appearances for the United States.</p><p>"That front three haven't been together since the Olympic gold-medal match, that's a long time, and we cannot waste a single minute," U.S. coach Emma Hayes said. "We absolutely have to put the very best players together with every opportunity that we have. But the circumstances are slightly different. We have Mal, who is coming back last, and yes, she is competing and contributing to Chicago, but like Soph last camp, it is so important to get them into the environment to reconnect with their teammates."</p><p>The United States will play Brazil on June 6 in Sao Paulo and June 9 in Fortaleza.</p><p>Because the national team does not play many friendly matches away from the United States, the games in Brazil give the younger players an opportunity to experience travel routines.</p><p>Additionally, Brazil is hosting next year's Women's World Cup. The United States will attempt to qualify for the tournament starting in late November at the CONCACAF W Championship.</p><p>"This is another moment where we get to see how we cope with all of the environmental conditions that come with going to Brazil, whether that's adapting to different cultures, different training facilities, different hotels, different experiences, fan experience, feeling like the away team, but with the pressure cooker of a top opponent. All of these things really, really matter," Hayes said.</p><p>Hayes named 26 players to the camp roster for the international window, with 23 players to be designated as available for each match.</p><p><b>Goalkeepers:</b> Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign), Mandy McGlynn (Utah Royals), Phallon Tullis-Joyce (Manchester United)</p><p><b>Defenders:</b> Tierna Davidson (Gotham), Emily Fox (Arsenal), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash), Lilly Reale (Gotham), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit), Emily Sonnett (Gotham), Gisele Thompson (Angel City), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave)</p><p><b>Midfielders:</b> Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current), Lindsey Heaps (OL Lyonnes), Claire Hutton (Bay FC), Riley Jackson (North Carolina Courage), Rose Lavelle (Gotham), Olivia Moultrie (Portland Thorns), Jaedyn Shaw (Gotham), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes)</p><p><b>Forwards:</b> Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit), Emma Sears (Racing Louisville), Ally Sentnor (Kansas City Current), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns).</p><p></p><h3>Stars dismiss GM</h3><p>The Stars and general manager Richard Feuz have parted ways, the team announced on Wednesday. </p><p>“Chicago Stars FC and its ownership recognize that our on-field performance has fallen short of the standards we have set for ourselves and the expectations of our fans,” Stars president Karen Leetzow said in a statement on the team's website. “Following a thorough assessment of the organization, we have determined that a change in sporting leadership is necessary to reach our collective ambitions."</p><p>The Stars are in 15th place with a 3-8-0 record and nine points, ahead of only 16th place Racing Louisville.</p><p>The team went 16-34-13 in the regular season and 17-36-14 overall since Feuz joined the club in February 2024. The Stars reached the playoffs in 2024. </p>

entries.title: Julieta Venegas, Common, Beach Bunny y Babyface encabezarán el regreso de Taste of Chicago
entries.summary: <p>El Taste of Chicago se expandirá a cinco días y regresará al corazón del verano, con docenas de restaurantes y artistas destacados como Julieta Venegas, Babyface, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2023/08/23/beach-bunnys-lili-trifilio-talks-salt-shed-pool-party" target="_blank" >Beach Bunny</a> y <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2024/01/29/chicago-native-common-tackles-self-help-in-his-new-book" target="_blank" >Common</a>, anunció el departamento de asuntos culturales de la ciudad el jueves de la semana pasada.</p><p>El festival gastronómico gratuito se llevará a cabo del 8 al 12 de julio en Grant Park. En los últimos años, el evento se había trasladado a septiembre para acomodar la carrera de NASCAR por las calles de Chicago, que no se llevará a cabo este año.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-610000" name="module-610000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Taste of Chicago es una de las tradiciones veraniegas más queridas de la ciudad porque refleja el corazón y el alma de Chicago a través de nuestra gente, nuestra cultura y nuestro extraordinario talento culinario”, dijo el alcalde Brandon Johnson en un comunicado.</p><p>Artistas destacados adicionales incluyen al cantante jamaiquino Original Koffee. entries.title: Para migrantes de Chicago, nuevas reglas y retrasos dificultan obtener y mantener un permiso de trabajo
entries.summary: <p>Jean Yameogo solía reunirse con amigos después del trabajo para tomar té y hablar de política.</p><p>Un día, dijo, alguien lo denunció por haber expresado una opinión negativa sobre el gobierno de Burkina Faso ante miembros de un grupo progubernamental.</p><p>Poco después, Yameogo contó que el grupo comenzó a amenazarlo. Fueron a su tienda de diseño de interiores en Ouagadougou, donde empleaba a tres personas, y destruyeron el equipo de soldadura y carpintería que usaba, así como materiales para coser y tapizar. Más tarde, le quemaron el automóvil.</p><p>“Tenía miedo”, cuenta Yameogo. “Tenía miedo por mi vida, también por la de mi familia”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e90000" name="module-e90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las amenazas surgieron en medio de un clima más amplio de miedo. Afirma que amigos fueron obligados a unirse al ejército para combatir a los terroristas tras criticar abiertamente al gobierno.</p><p>Así que Yameogo llegó a Estados Unidos con una visa de turista junto a su esposa, Coulibaly, y su hijo de tres años y solicitó asilo el 11 de diciembre de 2024. Su esposa regresó más tarde a Burkina Faso, mientras estaba embarazada, para visitar a unos parientes. Mientras estaba allí, los mismos hombres que lo habían atacado fueron a su casa y la agredieron, y perdió al bebé.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jean Yameogo dice que grupos progubernamentales incendiaron su automóvil tras criticar al gobierno de Burkina Faso.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ahora, Yameogo y su familia están viviendo en Cicero mientras espera que el gobierno de Estados Unidos decida su caso de asilo. Normalmente, los solicitantes de asilo pueden solicitar un permiso de trabajo temporal y obtenerlo después de aproximadamente seis meses, mientras su caso avanza en la corte. Pero Yameogo no ha podido obtener un permiso de trabajo.</p><p>Ha solicitado autorización de trabajo en varias ocasiones, pero sus solicitudes han sido negadas. Sally Schulze, portavoz de Refugee One, agencia sin fines de lucro que lo está ayudando con su caso, dice que no está segura por qué sus solicitudes fueron negadas, pero que el problema parece haber comenzado con una cita perdida con las autoridades de inmigración. Yameogo no recibió la notificación porque su familia se había mudado.</p><p>No contar con una dirección actualizada parece haberse convertido en una barrera de meses en un sistema colapsado, lo que puede resultar difícil de superar sin ayuda legal.</p><p>Sin un permiso de trabajo, Yameogo dice que ha luchado por proveer a su familia económicamente.</p><p>No está solo. Los defensores de los inmigrantes dicen que las políticas de la administración de Trump que apuntan a la autorización laboral están empujando a los inmigrantes fuera de la fuerza laboral legal. Esto incluye pausas en las solicitudes de permisos de trabajo de 39 países considerados "de alto riesgo", el fin de las extensiones automáticas de permisos de trabajo, tiempos de procesamiento más lentos para las solicitudes de permisos y una regla propuesta que haría más difícil que los solicitantes de asilo obtengan permisos de trabajo.</p><p>Esto es parte de un esfuerzo más amplio, dicen los defensores, para limitar las vías legales de los inmigrantes y presionarlos para que se autodeporten voluntariamente.</p><p>Los efectos, dicen algunos economistas, podrían ir más allá de los trabajadores inmigrantes y sus familias, extendiéndose a las empresas, empleadores y gobiernos locales cuando los trabajadores pierden ingresos o son empujados a trabajos informales.</p><p>Conchita Cruz, codirectora ejecutiva del Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, dice que algunos inmigrantes están luchando por obtener permiso de trabajo en primer lugar y otros corren el riesgo de perder ese permiso mientras renuevan permisos de trabajo que ya tenían.</p><p>“Los trabajadores inmigrantes con estatus de inmigración legal están saliendo de la fuerza laboral autorizada”, dijo.</p><h3>No más renovaciones automáticas</h3><p>En octubre, entró en vigor una regla que eliminó una salvaguarda que permitía a los trabajadores elegibles permanecer en su empleo mientras el Servicio de Ciudadanía e Inmigración de los Estados Unidos (USCIS) procesaba la renovación de su permiso de trabajo.</p><p>Antes, muchos trabajadores que solicitaban renovar a tiempo podían seguir trabajando hasta 540 días mientras la agencia federal procesaba la nueva tarjeta. Ahora, dice Cruz, muchos ya no obtienen esa extensión. Si su permiso vigente expira antes de que llegue el nuevo, los trabajadores podrían tener que dejar de trabajar incluso si presentaron la solicitud a tiempo.</p><p>Un portavoz de USCIS dice que la agencia está poniendo un nuevo énfasis en “un riguroso proceso de selección y verificación de extranjeros” antes de extender la autorización de trabajo.</p><p>La regla de octubre se aplica a los solicitantes en múltiples categorías de inmigración, incluidos algunos solicitantes de asilo y personas con Estatus de Protección Temporal (TPS). No se aplica a residentes permanentes legales, que pueden trabajar con una tarjeta de residente permanente o “green card”.</p><p>Una <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizen.org/wp-content/uploads/1-Complaint-18.pdf?" target="_blank" >demanda</a> que desafía la regla está avanzando en la corte.</p><h3>Un mercado laboral en la sombra</h3><p>Los economistas dicen que la política podría llevar a una pérdida de sueldos, una reducción del gasto, un aumento de los costos de contratación y una escasez de mano de obra.</p><p>En Illinois, la oficina del Fiscal General Kwame Raoul dice que la regla pone en riesgo a hasta 100,000 personas de perder sus empleos. La oficina de Raoul se unió a una coalición de fiscales generales para <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/News-Room/Current-News/12.1.25%20EAD%20Automatic%20Renew%20Comment%20Letter_State%20AGs.pdf?language_id=1" target="_blank" >presentar comentarios formales</a> al Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) en oposición a la regla.</p><p>“En el próximo año, cientos de miles de trabajadores inmigrantes, incluidos los solicitantes de asilo, sentirán las consecuencias del apresurado e ilegal movimiento del gobierno para eliminar las extensiones automáticas de los permisos de trabajo”, dice Cruz.</p><p>Los defensores y economistas dicen que cortar la autorización de trabajo puede empujar a las personas fuera de empleos estables y legales hacia un mercado laboral en la sombra con sueldos más bajos y protecciones laborales más débiles.</p><p>En Chicago, Enrique Espinoza, abogado de la clínica de inmigración del Chicago-Kent College of Law, dice que algunos de sus clientes han considerado abandonar Estados Unidos porque no pueden mantenerse mientras esperan, incluso si regresar a sus países podría ponerlos en riesgo.</p><p>“Siento que el gobierno realmente está presionando a fondo para ejercer más presión sobre esas personas que solo están tratando de cumplir con la ley”, dice Espinoza.</p><p>Si el permiso de trabajo de alguien expira antes de que llegue la renovación, los negocios podrían tener que reemplazar a personas que ya han entrenado, dice Espinoza.</p><p>“Van a tener que contratar a nuevas personas”, dice. “Va a costar más. Necesitan capacitar a estos nuevos empleados”.</p><h3>Atrasos, procesamiento lento</h3><p>La regla del permiso de trabajo ha provocado retrasos y tiempos de espera más largos para todo tipo de solicitudes de permisos de trabajo, según los defensores.</p><p>Félix Díaz, una residente de Cicero desde hace mucho tiempo y originaria de México, dice que durante años ha dependido de un permiso de trabajo vinculado a una petición federal bajo la Ley de Violencia contra las Mujeres después de sobrevivir a la violencia doméstica. Dice que ha renovado ese permiso durante más de una década, pero su última renovación, que solicitó en julio de 2025, no ha llegado, aunque recibió un aviso de USCIS diciendo que la solicitud fue recibida.</p><p>Su permiso de trabajo actual está programado para vencer en agosto. Si la nueva tarjeta no llega a tiempo, le preocupa que el negocio donde trabaja cuidando a personas mayores podría sacarla temporalmente del horario o incluso despedirla hasta que pueda demostrar una vez más que tiene una autorización laboral válida.</p><p>Díaz dice que comparte la renta y los gastos del hogar con sus hijos adultos, pero perder su propio sueldo aún amenazaría su independencia y aumentaría la presión en un hogar que ya enfrenta altos costos de vida.</p><p>“Estoy preocupada y estresada”, dice.</p><p>Si su empleador le pide documentos actualizados y no tiene el nuevo permiso, le preocupa que “me vayan a despedir”.</p><p>En febrero, la administración de Trump propuso una regla que eliminaría efectivamente los permisos de trabajo para la mayoría de los solicitantes de asilo, incluyendo Jean Yameogo. Si se implementa la regla, se impediría a los solicitantes de asilo trabajar legalmente mientras esperan que un juez decida su caso.</p><p>Yameogo tiene una audiencia en la corte de inmigración programada para septiembre. Está buscando “asilo defensivo”, que se aplica cuando una persona está en proceso de deportación y solicita asilo ante un juez para evitarla.</p><p>No importa lo que pase, dice que no puede regresar a Burkina Faso.</p><p>“No, no, nunca”, dice. “La situación no es buena”.</p><p>Yameogo llegó a Estados Unidos en busca de seguridad. Pero sin un permiso de trabajo, la seguridad no ha traído estabilidad.</p><p>Para ganar dinero, su esposa trenza cabello cuando puede. Yameogo acepta trabajos de construcción, pintura y otros trabajos pequeños cuando surgen.</p><p>Por ahora, tiene refugio del peligro del que huyó, pero no el permiso de trabajo que necesita para construir una vida más allá de la supervivencia.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Sky sign Saylor Poffenbarger to hardship contract amid wave of injuries
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> signed guard Saylor Poffenbarger to a hardship contract Tuesday. She'll be available for Wednesday's home game against the Tempo, the team said.</p><p>Poffenbarger went undrafted in 2026 but signed a training camp contract with the Lynx. She played college ball at UConn, Arkansas, and Maryland.</p><p>The Sky were down to nine active players before the signing. Leading scorer Rickea Jackson tore her ACL May 17 against the Lynx. Rookie Gabriela Jaquez hurt her left knee the same night, according to coach Tyler Marsh, but played in the next two games. </p><p>Jaquez is out for Wednesday's game and will be evaluated in one week, according to a team source.
